scenes.heading: Analysing substances in water
scenes.sub: What's in the water, and how much?
scenes.say: Some things dissolved in water are harmless. Others, like lead or arsenic, are dangerous at just a few parts per billion. So how do chemists measure what's there?

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: Darker car window tint lets less sunlight through
scenes.science: A more concentrated solution absorbs more light
scenes.breaks: tint blocks light fairly evenly, but a solution absorbs some wavelengths far more than others, so wavelength choice matters.
scenes.say: Think of tinted car windows. The darker the tint, the less sunlight gets through. In colorimetry, the coloured solution is the tint. The more concentrated it is, the more light it absorbs, so the absorbance goes up.

scenes.heading: Gravimetric analysis
steps: Dry to constant mass, then weigh
scenes.say: Gravimetric analysis means weighing the catch. Add an excess of a reagent so all the analyte forms a precipitate. Filter it, wash it, then dry it until its mass stops changing. Weigh it, and use stoichiometry to work back to the analyte.

scenes.heading: Worked example
scenes.question: Excess AgNO₃ is added to 250.0 mL of bore water. The dry AgCl weighs 0.574 g. Find [Cl⁻] in mg L⁻¹.
scenes.say: The silver chloride weighs zero point five seven four grams. Divide by its molar mass to get moles. The ratio is one to one, so that's the moles of chloride. Multiply by thirty-five point five, then divide by zero point two five litres: five hundred and sixty-eight milligrams per litre.
scenes.caption: The AgCl weighs 0.574 g. Divide by its molar mass to get moles. The ratio is 1 : 1, so that's the moles of chloride. Multiply by 35.5, then divide by 0.2500 L: 568 mg L⁻¹.

scenes.heading: Error check
points: Wet or unwashed: mass too high
scenes.say: Remember: wet and dirty weigh more; lost and dissolved weigh less. An undried or unwashed precipitate gives a result that's too high. Precipitate lost through the filter, or not all precipitated, gives a result that's too low.

scenes.heading: Calibration curves
points: Zero with a blank; measure at λmax
Read the unknown off the line
scenes.say: A calibration curve is a ruler you make yourself. Measure standards of known concentration, after zeroing with a blank, at the wavelength the solution absorbs most. Then read your unknown off the line. Stay inside your standards, and multiply by any dilution factor at the end.

scenes.heading: Atomic absorption (AAS)
points: Sample is atomised in a flame
Lamp made of the SAME element
Only that metal absorbs its light
scenes.say: Atomic absorption spectroscopy works like a lock and key. The lamp is made of the same element as the metal you're testing, so only that metal's atoms absorb its light. To test a different metal, change the lamp.

Quick recap. Gravimetric analysis weighs a dried precipitate. In colorimetry, more concentrated means more absorbance. Read calibration curves only within your standards. And A A S uses a lamp of the same element. Now try the practice questions!
